title: Particles and the States of Matter

blocks.text: Open a bottle of perfume at one end of a classroom in Ibadan and within a minute students at the back can smell it. Nobody carried it there. Invisible particles did the travelling, and that single observation is the foundation of all chemistry.

blocks.markdown:
## Matter is made of particles

Everything around you — the air, a bucket of water, a block of granite — is built from extremely small particles: atoms, molecules or ions. You cannot see them, but you can see what they do.

Two everyday observations prove it:

- **Diffusion** — the perfume spreading across the room, or a drop of ink colouring a whole beaker of water.
- **Brownian motion** — smoke particles viewed under a microscope jiggle randomly because invisible air molecules are hitting them from all sides.

blocks.title: Kinetic theory of matter
blocks.text: Matter is composed of tiny particles that are in continuous random motion. The particles attract one another, and the higher the temperature, the greater their average kinetic energy.

blocks.markdown:
### The three states

The *same* particles can exist in three states. What differs is how far apart the particles are, how strongly they are held and how freely they move.

Water is the classic example: ice, liquid water and steam are all H2O. Only the arrangement and energy of the molecules change.

blocks.caption: Comparing the three states of matter

blocks.markdown:
### Changes of state

Heating supplies energy that lets particles overcome the forces holding them together; cooling removes it.

- Solid to liquid: **melting** (reverse: freezing)
- Liquid to gas: **vaporisation / boiling** (reverse: condensation)
- Solid straight to gas: **sublimation** (reverse: deposition)

Ammonium chloride, iodine and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) all sublime — a favourite WAEC question.

blocks.title: Reading a heating curve
blocks.prompt: A pure solid is heated steadily. Its temperature rises, then stays constant at 80 degrees Celsius for four minutes, then rises again. What is happening during the flat portion, and what is the melting point?

steps.text: A flat portion on a heating curve means heat is still being supplied but the temperature is not rising.
That energy is being used to break the forces of attraction holding the particles in their fixed lattice positions, not to increase kinetic energy.
So the substance is melting: solid and liquid coexist throughout the flat section.
The constant temperature of the flat section is the melting point, and a sharp constant value confirms the solid is pure.

blocks.answer: The solid is melting; the melting point is 80 degrees Celsius, and the sharpness of the plateau shows the sample is pure.

blocks.title: Graham's law of diffusion
blocks.text: Lighter gases diffuse faster. The rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the square root of the density (or relative molecular mass) of the gas. This is why ammonia, with a molar mass of 17, travels down a tube faster than hydrogen chloride, with a molar mass of 36.5.

blocks.title: Answering state-of-matter questions
blocks.text: When asked to explain a property, always name the particle arrangement first and then the consequence. For example: 'a gas is highly compressible because its particles are very far apart, so there is a lot of empty space to squeeze out.' Marks are awarded for the link, not just the observation.

points: All matter is made of tiny particles in continuous random motion.
Diffusion and Brownian motion are direct evidence for the kinetic theory.
Solids have fixed shape and volume, liquids fixed volume only, gases neither.
Melting and boiling absorb energy to overcome forces of attraction; the temperature stays constant while the change occurs.
Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas, shown by iodine, ammonium chloride and dry ice.
